title: Breaking factor two for unrelated-machine makespan
formal: Do there exist a fixed real \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) and one uniform deterministic polynomial-bit-time algorithm that, on every valid unrelated-machine scheduling instance \(I\) defined below, outputs a feasible schedule \(\sigma\) with \[C_{\max}(\sigma)\le(2-\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}(I)?\] The machine count is part of the input, and \(\varepsilon\) is independent of it and of all processing times. No complexity assumption is included.
definitions:
For offline makespan minimization on unrelated parallel machines, define the real number
\[\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}=\inf\mathcal R,\qquad \mathcal R=\Bigl\{r\in[1,\infty):\exists A\ \exists c,k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall I\in\mathcal I,\ \begin{array}{l} A(I)\text{ halts in at most }c(L(I)+2)^k\text{ bit steps,}\\ A(I)\text{ outputs a feasible schedule }\sigma_I,\\ C_{\max}(\sigma_I)\le r\operatorname{OPT}(I)\end{array}\Bigr\}.\]
Here \(\mathcal I\) is the full class of finite rational processing-time matrices defined below, \(L(I)\) is the full binary input length, and \(A\) ranges over finite deterministic Turing-machine programs. 

An instance has integers \(m\ge1\), \(n\ge0\), machine set \([m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}\), job set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and a fully listed matrix \(p\in(\mathbb Q_{\ge0}\cup\{\infty\})^{m\times n}\). Set \([0]=\varnothing\). Each job has at least one finite entry. The symbol \(\infty\) forbids that machine–job assignment; it is not an arithmetic input with finite cost. Entries may differ arbitrarily between both machines and jobs. All processing times use the same time unit.

A feasible schedule is a function \(\sigma:[n]\to[m]\) such that \(p_{\sigma(j),j}<\infty\) for every job. Its load on machine \(i\) is \(\sum_{j:\sigma(j)=i}p_{ij}\), with an empty sum equal to zero. Define
\[C_{\max}(\sigma)=\max_{i\in[m]}\sum_{j:\sigma(j)=i}p_{ij},\qquad \operatorname{OPT}(I)=\min_{\sigma\text{ feasible}}C_{\max}(\sigma).\]
This minimum is finite and attained because the feasible set is finite and nonempty. Jobs are independent, available at time zero and indivisible. A machine executes its assigned jobs consecutively, one at a time, without preemption; their order does not affect the objective. There are no release dates, precedence constraints, setup times, communication costs or additional scheduling promises. For \(n=0\), the unique empty assignment has makespan zero.

Fix the following concrete binary encoding. For an integer \(u\ge0\), let \(b(u)\) be its binary expansion without leading zeros, with \(b(0)=0\), and put \(E(u)=1^{|b(u)|}0b(u)\), where juxtaposition denotes concatenation. A finite entry \(a/b\) is represented in lowest terms with \(a\ge0\), \(b\ge1\), as the tag bit \(0\) followed by \(E(a)E(b)\); \(\infty\) is the single tag bit \(1\). The input is \(E(m)E(n)\) followed by the \(mn\) entry encodings in row order. Its total bit length is \(L(I)\). The output is \(E(\sigma(1))\cdots E(\sigma(n))\) in job order; the empty schedule has an empty output. Equivalent ordinary encodings with polynomial-time translations give the same approximation-ratio infimum.

A program is a deterministic multitape Turing machine with no advice, random bits, optimization oracle or noncomputable constants. Input reading, work-tape computation and writing the full output count toward its bit running time. Arithmetic on the encoded rationals must be performed within that bound; an arbitrary-precision arithmetic operation is not a unit-cost primitive. Guarantees are required on every valid instance; invalid strings are outside \(\mathcal I\). The algorithm receives the complete matrix in advance, regardless of the category’s historical online-algorithms label.

For each fixed achieved ratio \(r\), the same program and constants \(c,k\) must work for all \(m,n,p\). They may depend on \(r\), but \(r\) is not additional advice or an input to the program. A different program for each input length is not allowed. The set \(\mathcal R\) concerns an absolute multiplicative guarantee on each instance, with no additive slack and no asymptotic or average-case exception. If \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)=0\), the output must also have makespan zero; no quotient by zero is used. All these conventions include empty instances.

The ratio is dimensionless. The established factor-two algorithm gives \(2\in\mathcal R\), so \(\mathcal R\) is nonempty and \(1\le\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}\le2\). The infimum need not be attained: \(\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}\le u\), for \(u\ge1\), means that for every \(\eta>0\) some program achieves a ratio at most \(u+\eta\), without requiring one program to attain \(u\) or one uniform procedure generating all these programs. A lower bound \(\ell\ge1\) means that no program achieves any fixed \(r\in[1,\ell)\) on every instance.
answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed assertion or of its logical negation, with exactly the stated model, quantifier order and parameter dependence. A bound for a restricted subclass or one particular algorithm is insufficient to refute a universal existence assertion. Determining the entire optimal rate or a numerical approximation to it is not required.
why: This is a central approximation question for allocating heterogeneous work to heterogeneous machines. The long gap between achievable guarantees and conditional hardness also has formal consequences for max-min fair allocation, making its resolution informative beyond scheduling.

progress.text: Lenstra–Shmoys–Tardos establish the factor-two polynomial-time algorithm, a scheme for fixed machine count, and hardness for every ratio below \(3/2\) unless \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\).
Shchepin–Vakhania improve the guarantee to \(2-1/m\). The saving depends on the number of machines and vanishes in the unrestricted worst case.
Verschae–Wiese give a configuration-LP gap of two for unrelated graph balancing. The journal issue is dated August 2014; neither date is a later unrestricted algorithmic hardness result.
Bamas and coauthors prove the makespan-to-Santa-Claus reduction and the stated two-value special-case guarantees. The preprint record remains version 1.
The prediction-assisted preprint gives improved guarantees with accurate extra information and worst-case factor two. Its Theorem 5.2 retains the search-budget dependence in its running time.
Feldman and coauthors’ revised Theorem 1 and Remark 4.1 distinguish the \(3/2\) fair-mechanism existence result from the polynomial transformation of a supplied initial allocation.

status_note: Source-open evidence checked on 15 September 2026. The SODA 2024 source explicitly leaves the unrestricted constant improvement unresolved; the inspected 2026 prediction, fair-mechanism and knapsack literature does not give an algorithm for the full model here. The known 3/2 lower bound assumes P differs from NP. The selected existence question imposes no such hypothesis and asks for some fixed improvement below factor two. The historical bounded search does not independently certify present openness.

context_blocks.text: The selected target restores the original source question: a polynomial-time \((2-\varepsilon)\)-approximation for one fixed universal \(\varepsilon>0\). It does not request a numerical determination of the full approximation-ratio infimum.

Unrelated machines need not have any common ranking by speed. A job can be fast on one machine and slow on another, while a second job has the reverse pattern. The makespan measures when all work has finished, so a schedule must balance indivisible loads rather than minimize their sum. Eligibility restrictions are included by forbidding selected assignments.

Lenstra, Shmoys and Tardos prove a polynomial-time factor-two approximation and show that every fixed ratio below \(3/2\) would imply \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\). Their hardness already uses a finite positive-integer subcase. Thus the unconditional bounds here are \(1\le\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}\le2\); assuming \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\), they become \(3/2\le\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}\le2\). If \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\), the finite rational scheduling optimization admits exact polynomial-time search and \(\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}=1\). The hardness assumption cannot be omitted from the lower endpoint.

Shchepin and Vakhania achieve ratio \(2-1/m\) for \(m\) machines. The same formula is below two for each finite \(m\), but its supremum over all machine counts is two. It therefore gives no fixed universal improvement. Likewise, the polynomial approximation scheme of Lenstra, Shmoys and Tardos fixes the number of machines in advance; its running-time dependence is different from the single polynomial required for unbounded \(m\).

For a target time \(T\), the configuration linear program has one nonnegative variable \(y_{i,S}\) for each machine and each job subset \(S\) whose total processing time on that machine is at most \(T\). It requires \(\sum_S y_{i,S}=1\) for each machine and total fractional coverage one for every job. Verschae and Wiese show that the supremum of the integral optimum divided by the least feasible relaxation time is two, even when each job has at most two eligible machines with potentially different processing times. This is a statement about that relaxation, not an impossibility result for every polynomial-time algorithm.

Restricted assignment requires a job to have the same processing time on every eligible machine. The SODA 2024 work of Bamas and coauthors gives a \((7/4+\delta)\)-approximation for its two-size subcase. For general two-value matrices with entries in \(\{u,w,\infty\}\), it gives \(2-1/n^{\delta}\) for every fixed \(\delta>0\), where \(n\) is the number of jobs. The exponent is on \(n\), not on the whole ratio. These guarantees preserve their restrictions and instance-size dependence.

The same paper proves that a polynomial-time \((2-1/\alpha)\)-approximation for unrestricted makespan, for any fixed \(\alpha\ge2\), yields a polynomial-time \((\alpha+\delta)\)-approximation for general Santa Claus allocation for every fixed \(\delta>0\). In that problem indivisible items have nonnegative player-dependent values, and the objective is to maximize the minimum total value received by a player. The reduction preserves the algorithmic significance of any fixed improvement here; the paper’s converse equivalence is confined to the two-value variants.

Baba, Bampis and Mitropoulos’ June 2026 preprint supplies an additional predicted partial job assignment. Its guarantee improves when prediction errors relative to an optimum are small and retains a worst-case factor two. The stated running time has a factor \((mn)^K\), so the search budget \(K\) must remain fixed for its polynomial-time claim. The inspected model uses positive processing times; neither good predictions nor a growing budget are supplied by the classical target.

The \(3/2\) result in Proportionally Fair Makespan Approximation concerns a mechanism’s fairness guarantee using an optimal initial allocation. The June 2026 revision explicitly states that its transformation is polynomial time given an allocation, while obtaining an optimal initial allocation is NP-hard. Consequently this existence result does not establish \(\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}\le3/2\). Fairness or incentive constraints and their separate existence bounds must be distinguished from computing a schedule with the complete polynomial-time guarantee in this card.
